Kurios
KOO-ree-os
n. (Greek)
Greek kurios, “lord, master, owner,” the great LXX/NT translation of the Hebrew YHWH (the divine Name, rendered the LORD in the KJV) and Adonai (Lord); also used of Jesus Christ in the NT as His distinctive divine title.

Biblical Definition

Kurios is the great Greek title of lordship—the word used in the LXX to translate both the divine Name YHWH (rendered the LORD in the KJV) and the Hebrew title Adonai (Lord), and used in the New Testament as Jesus’s distinctive divine title. The Christological weight is enormous. When the New Testament writers call Jesus kurios, they are not using a polite social honorific (though the word can carry that lesser sense in some contexts); they are using the very word their Greek-reading Bibles used for God Himself. The early Christian confession Jesus is Lord (kurios Iēsous) is therefore in its first-century context a confession of His deity, His co-identity with the LORD of the Old Testament, and His authority over all creation. Paul makes the equation explicit: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (kurios Iēsous Christos), to the glory of God the Father (Phil 2:10-11)—quoting Isaiah 45:23, where the One before whom every knee bows is YHWH Himself, and applying it directly to Jesus Christ as kurios. Romans 10:9: that if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. The confession of Jesus as Lord is the saving confession because it is the recognition of His deity and the submission to His authority that grace produces in the heart. The early church’s persecutors knew exactly what the confession claimed: the Roman demand that Christians say Caesar is Lord (kurios Kaisar) and the martyrs’ refusal—kurios Iēsous, not kurios Kaisar—was the political-theological flashpoint that put many of them to death. Beyond the Christological weight, kurios functions across the New Testament in its full lordship-sense. The Lord whose will is to be done; the Lord whose word is to be obeyed; the Lord whose service is the saint’s vocation; the Lord whose return is to be awaited; the Lord who will judge the living and the dead. The recovery of the title in its full biblical weight is structural to recovered Christian discipleship: Jesus is not merely Savior (a doctrine the lordship-truncated gospel of certain contemporary traditions emphasizes alone) but Lord, and the same Jesus who saved is the Lord whose authority over the saint is comprehensive.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Kurios: lord, master, owner; the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew divine Name YHWH and for the title Adonai; Jesus’s distinctive NT divine title, the confession Jesus is Lord being the early Christian recognition of His deity and authority over all creation.

expand to see more

LORD, n. — 1. A master; a person possessing supreme power and authority. 2. In the scripture, the Supreme Being; Jehovah. When LORD is in small capitals, it represents the Hebrew Jehovah. When written Lord, it represents the Hebrew Adonai. In the New Testament Lord answers to the Greek Kurios, and is applied especially to Jesus Christ as the divine title confessing His deity.

KURIOS — (Greek noun.) Lord, master, owner. The LXX translation of YHWH (rendered LORD) and Adonai (rendered Lord); in the NT, Jesus’s distinctive divine title (over 700 uses).

Key Scripture

Philippians 2:9-11 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

Romans 10:9 — "That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved."

1 Corinthians 12:3 — "Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost."

Acts 2:36 — "Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ."

Modern Corruption

Kurios is corrupted, on one side, by the lordship salvation controversy of certain contemporary traditions that have separated Savior from Lord and made Christ’s lordship optional to His saviorhood—and on the other by the casual contemporary use of Lord Jesus as a polite religious phrase shorn of the deity-confessing, authority-establishing weight the early Christian use of kurios Iēsous carried as the political-theological flashpoint of martyrdom.

expand to see more

The lordship salvation controversy of recent decades exposed a long-running corruption in certain evangelical traditions that had separated Savior from Lord: the gospel was preached as accept Jesus as Savior, with the question of His lordship over the saint’s life deferred or left optional. The biblical pattern refuses the separation. Romans 10:9 makes the confession kurios Iēsous structural to saving faith: the same Jesus who is Savior is Lord, and the confession of Him as Lord is the recognition of His deity, His authority, and the saint’s submission to Him as such. The recovery is the recovery of the integrated gospel: Christ is Savior and Lord in one indivisible person, and the saving confession received Him as such. The contemporary truncated gospel that omits His lordship has produced what its critics rightly called cheap grace: a Christianity in which Jesus is acknowledged as helpful for the afterlife while the present life is conducted as if His lordship over it had never been established.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the casual use of Lord Jesus as a polite religious phrase shorn of the deity-confessing, authority-establishing weight the early Christian use of kurios Iēsous carried. The martyrs of the early centuries went to lions and to fire for the refusal to say kurios Kaisar and the insistence on kurios Iēsous; the political-theological flashpoint of that confession was its explicit denial of Caesar’s ultimate lordship and its insistence that Jesus alone is Lord. Contemporary believers often invoke the same title without any sense of its weight: Lord Jesus as a verbal habit in prayer, the Lord as a religious code-word, Lord and Savior as a familiar phrase—but with no operative sense that the confession is the recognition of a deity, the establishment of an authority, the political-theological staking of one’s allegiance against every rival lord. Recover both ends. Refuse the lordship-omitting truncated gospel, and refuse the casual emptying of the deity-confession that kurios Iēsous in its first-century context carried. Jesus is Lord—the LORD of the Old Testament, the only Lord, the Lord whose authority over the saint’s life is comprehensive, the Lord whose return is the consummating event of history. The confession is everything, and the church saturated with the confession in its full weight is the church the apostles built and the martyrs died for.

Hebrew Roots

Greek kurios (lord, master, owner): the LXX translation of the Hebrew divine Name YHWH (rendered LORD) and the title Adonai; in the NT, Jesus’s distinctive divine title (over 700 uses), the confession kurios Iēsous being the early Christian recognition of His deity, authority, and saviorhood in one indivisible person.

expand to see more

Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, master, owner (over 700 NT uses).

Hebrew YHWH (H3068) — the divine Name, Yahweh / Jehovah (LXX usually translates with kurios; KJV usually renders LORD).

Hebrew Adonai (H136) — Lord (LXX also translates with kurios; KJV usually renders Lord).

Greek despotēs (G1203) — despot, master (a related but distinct title, emphasizing absolute ownership; 2 Pet 2:1; Jude 4 of Christ; Acts 4:24; Rev 6:10 of God the Father).

Usage

"That every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father—Phil 2:11 applies Isa 45:23 to Christ as kurios."

"No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost—the Spirit-wrought confession of Christ’s deity and lordship is the foundational mark of regenerate life."

"Lordship-omitting gospel separates Savior from Lord; casual contemporary use empties the confession of its deity-weight; biblical kurios Iēsous is the integrated recognition of Christ’s deity, saviorhood, and authority in one indivisible person."
